tool.dropTitle: Drop Defender's folders, its event log or a collection
tool.dropHint: Defender's Quarantine, DetectionHistory and Support folders, its Operational event log, MpCmdRun.log and the SOFTWARE hive, or a .zip, .tar.gz or folder holding them (KAPE WindowsDefender + RegistryHivesSystem, Velociraptor).
tool.sampleNote: The sample is FIN-WKS-07, a Windows 11 workstation on the day a rogue account staged tools: Defender caught one, was asked to switch off, and was told to ignore a folder. As KAPE collects it. Everything in it is synthetic: the quarantined files are harmless text and the threat names are made up.
tool.privacy: Runs entirely in your browser: files are never uploaded.
tool.nothingFound: Nothing to read was found in what you dropped. Drop Defender's folders (C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender), its Operational event log, MpCmdRun.log, the SOFTWARE hive, or the root of a collection (the folder that holds C\ProgramData and C\Windows).
tool.handoffFailed: {tool} did not send the files. Open them again from {tool}, or drop them here.
tool.search: Search threats, paths, users, hashes, settings…
tool.footNote: Times are UTC unless marked: MpCmdRun.log and some MPLog lines carry no zone.
tool.noDetections: No detection was found in what you dropped.
tool.from_inferred: name inferred from the documentation's order
tool.find_scope: Defender records what it detected and what was changed in its settings. A clean result is not proof that nothing ran: excluded folders and processes, anything Defender does not detect and anything that ran while it was off leave no detection. Compare with the execution artifacts.
tool.find_missing: Not in what you dropped: {list}. Those sources are not joined.
tool.find_none: Nothing stands out in what was read.
tool.find_note: Findings point at what deserves a look first; they are not verdicts. Severity here is the tool's, not Defender's.
tool.detail_userNote: As the source records it. Defender's Detection User is often NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM even when a person's action led to the detection.
tool.detail_noJoins: Only one source records this detection.
tool.join_history_detection_id: DetectionHistory file: same Detection ID {id} (its file name)
tool.join_history_quarantine_id: Quarantine entry: named by the DetectionHistory file ({id})
tool.join_quarantine_threat_path_time: Quarantine entry: same threat and path, {seconds} s from the detection
tool.join_mplog_threat_path_time: MPLog line {line}: same threat and path, {seconds} s from the detection
tool.join_mplog_threat_time: MPLog line {line}: same threat, {seconds} s from the detection
tool.join_mplog_same_detection: MPLog line {line}: same threat and path within a minute of the other lines
tool.join_sdn_same_path: MPLog line {line}: cloud query for the same path, {seconds} s before the detection
tool.detail_noEvents: No event in the Operational log.
tool.detail_quarantineNote: The Quarantine tab describes the content and recovers it as an encrypted ZIP.
tool.detail_cmdNote: MpCmdRun.log writes its times without a zone (the machine's local time): they are shown as written and are not on the UTC timeline.
tool.timeFrom_history: initial detection time of the DetectionHistory file
tool.field_keyTimeNote: shared by every value of the key
tool.q_intro: Each entry is what Defender moved into its quarantine (Entries\{GUID}): the threat, when, and each resource with its path, size and times. Where the ResourceData file was collected, its RC4 layer is removed in your browser to describe it: the streams Windows' BackupRead wrote, the file's size and hashes, its owner and its Zone.Identifier stream (where it was downloaded from). The file itself is never shown.
tool.q_magicMissing: magic numbers not found (read by its section sizes)
tool.q_noContent: The content (ResourceData\<xx>\<content ID>) was not in what you dropped.
tool.q_contentError: The content could not be read: {error}
tool.q_name_content: equals the SHA-1 of the whole decrypted content, as on the sample Yamato Security and maldump examined
tool.q_name_file: equals the SHA-1 of the recovered file
tool.q_name_none: equals neither SHA-1 here; the naming rule comes from few samples, so this alone does not mean the content was altered
tool.q_hiveNote: The content is a registry hive (a quarantined key or service): described, not offered for download.
tool.q_sparseNote: The data is stored as sparse blocks: this tool does not rebuild it.
tool.q_noZone: None in the quarantined content: nothing here records where the file came from.
tool.q_zipNote: The file is decrypted in your browser and saved only inside a ZIP encrypted with the password "{password}" (traditional ZIP encryption, which 7-Zip, unzip and Windows tools open), with its other streams and a README. Open it only on an isolated analysis machine.
tool.q_ack: I understand this file is malware and will handle it in an isolated environment.
tool.q_recoverMissing: The content file is no longer loaded: drop it again.
tool.q_recoverNone: This content holds no recoverable file (a registry hive or a sparse file).
tool.ch_intro: Changes to Defender's protection: the Operational log's configuration, tamper-protection, real-time protection, quarantine and history events; the exclusions and switches of the SOFTWARE hive at their key's LastWrite time; and every MpCmdRun.exe run, at its local time as written.
tool.reg_title: Defender keys in the SOFTWARE hive
tool.reg_intro: Only these keys are read: Microsoft\Windows Defender and Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender, with their Exclusions, Real-Time Protection, Spynet and Features subkeys. A key's LastWrite time dates the latest change to the key, not each value. Devices managed by Defender for Endpoint may not keep readable exclusions here: an empty Exclusions key is not proof that there are none.
tool.reg_none: None of these keys is in the hive.
tool.mp_intro: Defender's support logs, read line by line: each entry keeps its raw text, line number and type. Lines ending in Z are UTC; lines without a zone are shown as written, marked "no zone", and kept off the UTC timeline (their zone is not settled: sources disagree). SDN (cloud query) lines name files Defender looked up, with SHA-1 and SHA-256 in some versions; ProcessImageName lines name programs it scanned files for, detected or not.
tool.mp_noLogs: No MPLog or MPDetection file was read.
tool.mp_filesNote: From the cloud (SDN) query lines: a file Defender scanned and looked up, with its hashes when the line has them. Being here does not mean it was detected.
tool.mp_processesNote: From the estimated-impact lines: a program Defender scanned files for, with how many files. Being here shows the program ran; it does not mean it was detected.
tool.tl_note: Every record with a UTC time: Operational events, DetectionHistory times, quarantine entries, MPLog lines with a zone, and each Defender key's LastWrite once (the key's time, shared by its values).
tool.tl_unzoned: Not placed (no zone): {mplog} MPLog entries, {commands} MpCmdRun runs.
tool.tl_key: Defender key last written ({n} values share this time)
tool.files_intro: Each file: what it was read as, its encoding, its records, what was not understood and notes.
tool.files_approx: approximate: a ZIP's DOS time, zone unknown
tool.files_ignored: {n} other files in the collection were not opened (not one of the Defender files or the SOFTWARE hive).
tool.files_unparsedNote: Lines with no time outside a known block; the entries around them were read.
tool.note_evtx_not_read: Not read by the EVTX reader.
tool.note_evtx_capped: Only the first {n} of {total} records were read.
tool.note_evtx_other_provider: {n} records come from another provider than Defender.
tool.note_history_not: Does not start like a DetectionHistory file.
tool.note_history_name_differs: Its Detection ID ({id}) differs from its file name.
tool.note_q_no_magic: The header's magic numbers are missing; read by its section sizes.
tool.note_q_crc: A section's CRC-32 differs from its content (either way of storing it).
tool.note_q_name_differs: Its GUID ({id}) differs from its file name.
tool.note_rd_name_content: Its name is the SHA-1 of the whole decrypted content.
tool.note_rd_name_file: Its name is the SHA-1 of the recovered file.
tool.note_rd_name_none: Its name is neither SHA-1 computed here.
tool.note_rd_hive: The content is a registry hive.
tool.note_rd_sparse: The data is sparse: not rebuilt.
tool.note_rd_no_entry: No quarantine entry in what you dropped names this content.
tool.note_cut: Only the first part of the file was read (size or line limit).
tool.note_mplog_dropped: {n} more entries past the per-file limit were counted, not kept.
tool.note_mplog_no_zone: {n} entries carry a time without a zone: shown as written, not on the timeline.
tool.note_mplog_other: {n} timed lines of types the tool does not name are kept as "other".
tool.note_encoding_unexpected: Read as {encoding}; Defender writes this file in {expected}. A converted copy?
tool.note_cmd_local_time: Times are the machine's local time as written, zone not recorded.
tool.note_hive_dirty: The hive was not cleanly written back: recent changes may sit in its .LOG1/.LOG2 files, which are not replayed.
tool.note_hive_truncated: The hive is shorter than its header says: keys past the cut are missing.
tool.note_no_defender_keys: No Windows Defender key in this hive.
tool.note_not_read: A Defender file this tool does not read.
tool.skip_notRead: Defender's SQLite database (mpenginedb.db, {size}): not read by this tool
tool.ev_1127: Controlled folder access blocked a sector write
tool.why_staging_path: Temporary folders, C:\Users\Public, the recycle bin, PerfLogs and first-level ProgramData folders are writable by every user or emptied often. Installed software does not live there; a dropped tool or a payload unpacked from an archive often does.
tool.group_staging_path: Detected in a temporary or shared folder
tool.why_downloads: The detected file sat in a Downloads folder: something fetched from the internet or saved from mail. Common for unwanted software, and the usual first step of an intrusion that starts with a download.
tool.why_action_failed: Defender could not complete its action (event 1118 or 1119, an older 1008, a DetectionHistory status ending in 'failed', or an error code on 1117). The file or process may still be on the machine, or running.
tool.why_action_allowed: The action recorded is Allow or No action, or the DetectionHistory status is Allowed: the threat was detected and left in place, by a user's choice or by a policy (ThreatSeverityDefaultAction). Defender's documentation notes these actions do not remediate.
tool.why_amsi: The detection came through the Antimalware Scan Interface: a script engine (PowerShell, VBScript, JScript, Office macros) handed content to Defender before running it. The threat was code in memory or in a script, not necessarily a file. AMSI is told by the event's own Source Name, an 'amsi' resource, or Source ID 10, whose name follows the order of Defender's event documentation.
tool.why_same_hash: The same SHA-256 (or SHA-1) was detected at several paths: one file copied around, renamed or dropped again.
tool.why_exclusion_nearby: An exclusion that covers this detection was added within an hour of it (by its 5007 event, or by the LastWrite time of the exclusion key). Someone made Defender ignore what it had just caught, or prepared the ground for it. A path exclusion covers what is under the folder, an extension exclusion the file's extension, and a process exclusion by name the process that touched the file or the detected file's own name.
tool.flag_recent: Within 7 days of the newest record ({date})
tool.why_recent: Within 7 days before the newest UTC record of this host.
tool.group_recent: Within 7 days of the newest record
tool.why_exclusion_drive_root: The exclusion covers a drive root or every path: Defender scans nothing there.
tool.why_exclusion_writable: The excluded folder is one any user can write to (C:\Users, C:\ProgramData, temporary folders, Downloads, AppData). Anything dropped there runs unscanned. Vendors sometimes ask for such exclusions; an intruder adds them to protect their tools.
tool.why_exclusion_broad_ext: The excluded extension covers most programs or scripts (.exe, .dll, .ps1, .bat, .js…): every file with it is skipped, wherever it is.
tool.flag_exclusion_script_host: Script host or system program excluded: {value}
tool.why_exclusion_script_host: A process exclusion makes Defender skip the files that process opens. Excluding PowerShell, cmd.exe, the Windows Script Host, mshta, rundll32 and their kin lets anything they load run unscanned.
tool.why_exclusion_process_name: A process exclusion given as a file name with no folder applies to a process of that name wherever it runs (Defender's exclusion documentation): copying any program to that name makes the files it opens go unscanned.
tool.why_exclusion_other: An exclusion that matches none of the broader rules. Exclusions are a normal tool for administrators; each one is a place Defender does not look.
tool.why_exclusion_near_detection: This exclusion covers a file Defender detected within an hour of it being added (by its 5007 event, or by the LastWrite time of its key, which every value of the key shares). Excluding what was just caught is a common next step for an intruder whose tool was quarantined.
tool.why_rtp_off: Event 5001: real-time protection, the scanning of files as they are opened and written, was disabled. Check which setting changed (5007, 5004) and the command that did it (PowerShell logs, MpCmdRun.log).
tool.why_scanning_off: Event 5010 or 5012: antispyware or antivirus scanning was disabled.
tool.why_setting_off: A Disable… switch of Defender is set to 1 in the registry, or a 5007 event recorded it changing to 1: a protection feature is off.
tool.why_tamper_off: The TamperProtection value under Features reads as off. This value is not officially documented: one public source (Bhabesh Raj), echoed by community write-ups and Elastic's tampering rule, reads 5 as on and 4 (or 0) as off.
tool.why_maps_off: SpynetReporting is 0: Defender does not consult its cloud protection service.
tool.why_tamper_blocked: Event 5013: tamper protection refused a change to Defender's settings. The change did not happen, but someone or something tried; the value names what was attempted.
tool.why_quarantine_restored: Event 1009 (or MpCmdRun -Restore): a quarantined item went back to disk. Find who restored it and whether it ran.
tool.why_quarantine_deleted: Event 1011: a quarantined item was removed from the quarantine. Defender also purges old items on its own; the user field tells who.
tool.why_history_deleted: Event 1013: Defender's history of detections was deleted. Defender also purges old history on its own; deleting it by hand removes the record of what was found.
tool.why_remove_definitions: MpCmdRun.exe was run to roll back security intelligence (-All restores the original set): a known way to blind Defender to recent threats.
tool.why_mpcmdrun_tamper: MpCmdRun.exe was run with an option that changes what Defender detects or runs (dynamic signatures, platform reset or revert) or downloads a file (-DownloadFile, a known misuse).

collect.title: Collect Defender's files and keys
collect.intro: Defender's folders under C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender are readable by administrators and SYSTEM only. The Operational event log is open while Windows runs: export it. The SOFTWARE hive is locked: save it or take it from a triage tool.
collect.step1: Copy the folders, export the log
collect.step2: Drop the folder or the archive here
collect.step3: Read in your browser, never uploaded
collect.copyNote: From an elevated Command Prompt. robocopy /B (backup mode) reads the folders whatever their permissions; /XD skips the large Definition Updates folder. wevtutil epl exports the Operational log (any file name with "Defender" and .evtx is recognised). reg save writes the SOFTWARE hive. Keeping the C\ProgramData\… and C\Windows\… layout under a folder named after the host lets the tool place the files. In a batch file, double the % of %u and %~nxu.
collect.kapeNote: The WindowsDefender target collects the Operational log, the Support folder, MpCmdRun.log, DetectionHistory and the Quarantine; RegistryHivesSystem adds SOFTWARE. WinDefendDetectionHist collects DetectionHistory alone. Drop the zip here.
collect.velociraptorNote: Collect Windows.KapeFiles.Targets (Windows.Triage.Targets in recent releases) with the WindowsDefender and RegistryHivesSystem targets, then drop the collection's zip here: Velociraptor's C%3A folder names are understood.
collect.powershellNote: To look on a live machine without copying, as an administrator. Get-MpThreatDetection lists what DetectionHistory holds; Get-MpPreference the current exclusions and switches (exclusions are shown to administrators only); Get-MpComputerStatus whether tamper protection is on.
collect.whereNote: ResourceData and Resources files are named by a 40-hex-digit content ID, in a subfolder named after its first two characters. DetectionHistory files are named by the detection's GUID.
collect.copyFailed: Copy failed: select the command and copy it by hand.
gotchas: The quarantine holds live malware, RC4-encrypted with a key that is public. Handle the copy as malware: store it encrypted, do not open it on a workstation.
Collect early: the Operational log rolls over, MPLog files rotate, Defender purges quarantined items and detection history after a while, and an intruder with administrator rights can delete them.
Your own antivirus may react to the collected files: ResourceData is encrypted, but the logs name threats.
mpenginedb.db (Defender's SQLite database in Scans) is not read by this tool.

what: Defender Antivirus, built into Windows 10 and 11, keeps several records of its work: an event log, plain-text support logs, one file per detection, an encrypted quarantine that still holds what it caught, a log of its command-line tool, and its settings in the registry.

Read together, they say what was detected, where, by which process and user, what Defender did about it, and who weakened Defender before or after: a switch turned off, a blocked attempt, an exclusion added minutes after a tool was quarantined.
reference.filesTitle: The artifacts and where they live
files: Operational event log: C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender%4Operational.evtx. 1116 (detected) and 1117 (action taken) carry the threat, path, process, user, detection source and action; 1118/1119 a failed action; 5001, 5004, 5007, 5010, 5012 and 5013 settings changes and blocked attempts; 1009, 1011 and 1013 quarantine and history actions.

DetectionHistory: …\Windows Defender\Scans\History\Service\DetectionHistory\<nn>\<GUID>, one binary file per detection, named by its Detection ID: threat, resources with tracking data (hashes, size), user, process, status and the quarantine entry it went to.

Quarantine: …\Windows Defender\Quarantine\Entries\{GUID} (the threat, when, and each resource with its path, size and times), ResourceData\<xx>\<ID> (the content: what Windows' BackupRead returned for the file, RC4-encrypted) and Resources\<xx>\<ID> (which entries hold a content).

MPLog and MPDetection: …\Windows Defender\Support\MPLog-*.log, MPDetection-*.log. Defender's troubleshooting log: cloud (SDN) queries naming files with their hashes, programs it scanned files for, detections, exclusions, versions.
MpCmdRun.log: C:\Windows\Temp\MpCmdRun.log, and %TEMP%\MpCmdRun.log of a user who ran MpCmdRun.exe: each run's command line and times.

SOFTWARE hive: Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions (Paths, Extensions, Processes, IpAddresses, TemporaryPaths), Real-Time Protection, Spynet, Features (TamperProtection), and the same under Policies\Microsoft\Windows Defender.
reference.provesTitle: What they prove, and what they do not
proves: That a file or script content was present and detected, where, when, through which source (real-time, AMSI, download, scan) and what Defender did. A detection on write or download does not prove the file ran.
The quarantined file itself, with its owner and, when it had one, its Zone.Identifier stream: the zone and the URL it was downloaded from.
That a file existed, with its hashes, even when nothing was detected: MPLog's cloud queries and estimated-impact lines.
Defense evasion: exclusions, switches set to off, tamper-protection blocks (an attempt that failed), quarantine restores, history deletions, MpCmdRun options that roll back protection.
Absence proves little: excluded folders and processes, anything Defender does not detect and anything that ran while it was off leave no detection.
how: Everything is read in your browser, in a Web Worker. The Operational log goes through EVTX Parser's WebAssembly reader; every other format has its own bounded reader, fuzz-tested against damaged and crafted files.

Detections are joined: the log's events by Detection ID, the DetectionHistory file by the same ID (its name), the quarantine entry by the GUID the history file names (else by threat, path and time), MPLog's lines by threat, path and time. Each join shows its evidence.

Quarantine entries and ResourceData are decrypted with Defender's published RC4 key. The content is described (streams, size, MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, owner, Zone.Identifier) and never shown. It leaves the page only as a ZIP encrypted with the password "infected", on an explicit click.

Times: the event log, DetectionHistory, the quarantine and MPLog lines ending in Z are UTC. MPLog lines without a zone and MpCmdRun.log are shown as written and kept off the UTC timeline. Registry keys are dated by their LastWrite time, shared by all their values.
Files are placed on hosts by their collection path (KAPE's C\ folder, Velociraptor's C%3A, a host folder above them); loose files are recognised by name and content.
limits: Defender's events are officially documented, its files are not. The quarantine, DetectionHistory and MPLog layouts come from public research (Fox-IT, Orange Cyberdefense, libyal, Yamato Security, Intrinsec) and can change with Defender's platform versions; values whose meaning is not known are kept and shown as unnamed.
In the raw event log, some name fields (Source Name, Action Name…) hold message-table references such as %%818; the tool then names the ID from documented tables and says so.
The ResourceData file name matched the SHA-1 of the whole decrypted content on the samples examined publicly, not the file's own hash; few samples exist.
TamperProtection's values are not officially documented; 5 = on and 4 = off come from one public source.
Devices managed by Defender for Endpoint may not keep readable exclusions in the registry; an empty Exclusions key is not proof that there are none.
mpenginedb.db is not read, hive transaction logs are not replayed, sparse quarantined files are not rebuilt.
A flag is a reason to look, not a verdict.

faq.a: No. The page reads the files in your browser with JavaScript and WebAssembly in a Web Worker; nothing is sent to a server. You can disconnect from the network once the page has loaded.

faq.q: Is it safe to load a quarantine here?
faq.a: The quarantined content is decrypted in memory only to describe it and to hash it; it is never rendered, never run and never saved raw. If you ask for it, it is written into a ZIP encrypted with the password "infected". Treat that ZIP as live malware.

faq.q: Why does the detection time differ from the event's time?
faq.a: 1116 carries a Detection Time field; the event itself is written a moment later, and 1117 when the action finishes. The tool shows the Detection Time as the detection's time and keeps the event times with each event.

faq.q: Why are some MPLog lines not on the timeline?
faq.a: Lines ending in Z are UTC. Newer logs also write times without a zone, and public samples disagree on what zone those are in, so the tool shows them as written and leaves them off the UTC timeline. MpCmdRun.log writes local time without a zone too.

faq.q: An exclusion is in the registry: when was it added?
faq.a: The registry keeps one LastWrite time per key, shared by all its values: it dates the latest change to the key. A 5007 event, when the log still has it, dates each change and gives the old and new value.

faq.q: Can it read a disk image?
faq.a: Export the Defender folders, the Operational log, MpCmdRun.log and the SOFTWARE hive with Disk Image Parser or another forensic tool and drop the folder here. The page also accepts files handed over by Disk Image Parser, tab to tab, without a server.

privacyPage.title: Privacy policy
privacyPage.description: How Defender Parser handles your data: Defender files and registry hives are read in your browser and never uploaded; recovered quarantine files leave the browser only as the encrypted ZIP you download; no cookies.
summary: Files you analyse never leave your device: they are read in your browser, never uploaded.
Recovered quarantine files never leave your browser except as the password-protected ZIP you choose to download.
No accounts, no cookies, no advertising, no cross-site tracking.
Visits and a few anonymous usage events are measured without cookies; file names and contents are never sent.

p: {site} is operated by {org}. For any question about your data, write to {email}.

Files you open (Defender's quarantine, DetectionHistory and support logs, its event log, MpCmdRun.log, the SOFTWARE registry hive, or a .zip or .tar.gz collection of them) are read and processed by JavaScript and WebAssembly code running in your browser (in a Web Worker). They are not uploaded to us or to anyone else.

Quarantined files are decrypted in your browser's memory only to describe them (sizes, hashes, streams). They are never displayed, never run, and never leave your browser except inside the ZIP encrypted with the password "infected" that you download by an explicit click; that ZIP is saved by your browser to your device and is not sent anywhere.
Files handed over from Disk Image Parser in another tab go from that tab to this one inside your browser (with postMessage), without passing through any server.
From the registry hive, the tool reads only the Windows Defender keys (exclusions, real-time protection, cloud protection and tamper-protection settings, and their policy copies).
Exports you download (CSV, JSON, Markdown) are generated in your browser and never contain the content of quarantined files. Closing or reloading the page forgets everything you loaded.

sections.h: What is kept in your browser
list: Your theme choice (light or dark), in local storage.
p: None of this is sent to us. You can remove it at any time by clearing this site's data in your browser settings.

The site is hosted by Vercel Inc., which delivers the pages. Like any web server it processes technical data for each request: IP address, date and time, requested address, browser user agent and referring page. This is needed to deliver the site and to protect it against abuse (legitimate interest), and it is kept for a limited period under Vercel's retention rules. Vercel is based in the United States; see its privacy policy ({vercel}) for how transfers outside the EU are safeguarded.

We use Vercel Web Analytics to count page views and Vercel Speed Insights to measure loading performance (for example how fast pages display on a type of device). Neither uses cookies or tracks you across sites; visitors are not identified.

Web Analytics also records a few anonymous usage events, each with at most two coarse properties: files were analysed (whether they came from your device, the sample or a handover from another tool, never their names or content), the sample was loaded, a quarantined file was saved as an encrypted ZIP (never which one), a file was chosen or dropped (only its extension, such as evtx, log or zip, and whether it was chosen or dropped), an export format, a copy action (only whether it came from code, a table or a field, never the copied text), a search (never the query), and a link followed to another site (only its domain).
The purpose is to understand which pages and features are useful and to keep the site fast (legitimate interest).
The site sets no cookies. That is why there is no cookie banner.

Fonts, scripts, the analysis code (including its WebAssembly module) and the sample files are all served from this site. There is no advertising, no social-media widget and no embedded third-party content. Links to other sites take you to those sites, under their own policies.
We use your address and message only to reply, and keep them no longer than the exchange requires.

Under the GDPR you can ask for access to, correction or deletion of personal data about you, restrict or object to its processing, and ask for a copy (portability). Since the site has no accounts and never receives your files, there is usually very little we hold; write to {email} and we will answer within one month. You can also complain to your data-protection authority (in France, the CNIL).
If this policy changes, the new version is published on this page with its date.

termsPage.title: Terms of use
termsPage.description: The terms for using Defender Parser: a free, as-is analysis aid; your responsibility for the files you analyse and for any malware you recover; acceptable use.
summary: Free, no account, provided as it is.
Results are aids for an analyst, not verdicts.
Only analyse files you are entitled to handle; recovered quarantine files are live malware and are your responsibility.

p: {site} is a free website and analysis tool operated by {org}. Contact: {email}. By using the site you accept these terms.

{site} reads Microsoft Defender Antivirus artifacts (the quarantine, DetectionHistory, the support logs, the Operational event log, MpCmdRun.log and the Defender registry keys) in your browser, lists the detections and protection changes they record, and can recover a quarantined file into an encrypted ZIP on your request; it also publishes articles on the subject.
